title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter II
paragraphs:
“‘Dime; no ves aquel caballero que hacia nosotros viene sobre un
caballo rucio rodado que trae puesto en la cabeza un yelmo de oro?’ ‘Lo
que veo y columbro,’ respondio Sancho, ‘no es sino un hombre sobre un
as no pardo como el mio, que trae sobre la cabeza una cosa que
relumbra.’ ‘Pues ese es el yelmo de Mambrino,’ dijo Don
Quijote.”—CERVANTES.

“‘Seest thou not yon cavalier who cometh toward us on a dapple-gray steed, and weareth a golden helmet?’ ‘What I see,’ answered Sancho, ‘is nothing but a man on a gray ass like my own, who carries something shiny on his head.’ ‘Just so,’ answered Don Quixote: ‘and that resplendent object is the helmet of Mambrino.’”

“Sir Humphry Davy?” said Mr. Brooke over the soup, smiling in his easy way as he picked up Sir James Chettam's remark about studying Davy's Agricultural Chemistry. “Well, now, Sir Humphry Davy. I dined with him years ago at Cartwright's, and Wordsworth was there too—the poet Wordsworth, you know. There's a curious thing. I was at Cambridge at the same time as Wordsworth and never met him, and twenty years later I dined with him at Cartwright's. Things do turn out oddly. But Davy was there; he was a poet as well. Or you might say Wordsworth was poet number one, and Davy poet number two. True in every sense, you know.”

Dorothea felt rather more uneasy than usual. At the start of dinner, with so few people and such a quiet room, these specks shaken from the bulk of a magistrate's mind fell too conspicuously. How, she wondered, could a man like Mr. Casaubon bear such trivial conversation? His manner seemed very dignified to her. The arrangement of his iron-grey hair and his deep-set eyes reminded her of Locke's portrait. He had the lean figure and pale complexion appropriate to a scholar, utterly unlike the flourishing, red-whiskered English type embodied by Sir James Chettam.

“I'm reading Agricultural Chemistry,” said that excellent baronet, “because I intend to manage one of the farms myself and see whether I can set my tenants a good example of farming. Do you approve, Miss Brooke?”

“A great mistake, Chettam,” Mr. Brooke broke in. “Electrifying your land and that sort of thing, turning your cowshed into a drawing room. It won't do. I went deeply into science myself at one time, but I saw it wouldn't do. It leads you into everything; you can't leave anything alone. No, no—make sure your tenants don't sell their straw and that sort of thing, and give them drainage tiles, you know. But this fancy farming won't do. It's the dearest whistle you can buy; you might just as well keep a pack of hounds.”

“Surely,” said Dorothea, “it's better to spend money discovering how people can make the best use of the land that supports them all than on keeping dogs and horses merely to gallop across it. There is no sin in making yourself poor through experiments that benefit everyone.”

She spoke more forcefully than was expected of so young a lady, but Sir James had asked her. He often did, and she had often imagined encouraging him in many good deeds once he became her brother-in-law.
While Dorothea spoke, Mr. Casaubon turned his eyes pointedly towards her and seemed to notice her afresh.

“Young ladies don't understand political economy, you know,” Mr. Brooke said, smiling at Mr. Casaubon. “I remember when we all read Adam Smith. Now _there's_ a book. At one time I absorbed every new idea—human perfectibility, for instance. But some say history goes round in circles, and you can make a very good case for that; I've argued it myself. The truth is that human reason can take you a little too far—over the hedge, in fact. It took me quite a distance once, but I saw it wouldn't do. I reined in, reined in just in time. Not too sharply, though. I've always favoured a little theory. We must have Thought, or we'll find ourselves back in the dark ages. But speaking of books, there's Southey's ‘Peninsular War.’ I'm reading it in the mornings. Do you know Southey?”

“No,” said Mr. Casaubon, unable to keep up with Mr. Brooke's headlong reasoning and thinking only of the book. “At present I have little time for literature of that sort. Lately I have been wearing out my eyes over ancient scripts. In fact, I need someone to read to me in the evenings. But I am particular about voices and cannot bear listening to an inadequate reader. In some ways it is unfortunate: I draw too much nourishment from inward sources; I spend too much time among the dead. My mind is rather like an ancient man's ghost, wandering the world and trying to reconstruct it in thought as it once was, despite its ruins and bewildering changes. Still, I find I must take the greatest care of my eyesight.”

This was Mr. Casaubon's first extended speech. He spoke precisely, as if required to make a public statement. The neat, balanced rise and fall of his delivery, occasionally accompanied by a nod, stood out all the more against good Mr. Brooke's slovenly fragments. Dorothea told herself he was the most interesting man she had ever met, not even excepting Monsieur Liret, the Vaudois clergyman who had lectured on Waldensian history. To reconstruct a vanished world, surely in the service of truth's highest purposes—what work to witness in any capacity, to help with even by holding a lamp! That uplifting thought carried her above her annoyance at being teased about her ignorance of political economy, that science which was never explained and was brought down like a snuffer on every light she kindled.

“But you enjoy riding, Miss Brooke,” Sir James managed to say presently. “I would have thought you could appreciate some of the pleasures of hunting. I wish you'd let me send a chestnut horse over for you to try. He's been trained for a lady. On Saturday I saw you cantering over the hill on a horse quite unworthy of you. My groom can bring Corydon every day; you need only name the hour.”

“Thank you, you're very kind. I intend to give up riding. I won't ride again,” Dorothea said. She was driven to this abrupt decision by irritation that Sir James kept claiming her attention when she wanted to give it all to Mr. Casaubon.
“No, that's too harsh,” Sir James said, his reproachful tone revealing his keen concern. “Your sister is inclined to self-denial, isn't she?” he went on, turning to Celia on his right.
“I think she is,” Celia replied, afraid of saying something her sister would dislike and blushing as prettily as possible above her necklace. “She enjoys giving things up.”
“If that were true, Celia, giving things up would be self-indulgence for me, not self-denial. But there can be good reasons for choosing not to do something very pleasant,” Dorothea said.
Mr. Brooke was talking at the same moment, but Mr. Casaubon was clearly watching Dorothea, and she knew it.
“Exactly,” Sir James said. “You give things up for some noble, generous reason.”

“No, really, not exactly. I didn't say that about myself,” Dorothea replied, turning red. Unlike Celia she seldom blushed, and only from intense delight or anger. Just now it was anger at the contrary Sir James. Why couldn't he attend to Celia and let her listen to Mr. Casaubon? If only that learned man would talk instead of letting Mr. Brooke talk at him. Her uncle was explaining that the Reformation either meant something or it didn't; that he himself was Protestant to the core, but Catholicism was a fact; and as for refusing an acre of one's land for a Romanist chapel, all men needed religion's bridle, which, properly understood, meant fear of the Hereafter.

“I made quite a study of theology once,” Mr. Brooke said, as though accounting for the insight he had just displayed. “I know a little of every school. I knew Wilberforce in his best days. Do you know Wilberforce?”
Mr. Casaubon's answer was “No.”
“Well, perhaps Wilberforce wasn't enough of a thinker. But if I entered Parliament, as people have asked me to do, I'd sit as an independent, as Wilberforce did, and work for philanthropic causes.”
Mr. Casaubon inclined his head and remarked that the field was broad.

“Yes,” Mr. Brooke replied with an easy smile, “but I have documents. I started collecting them a long time ago. They need putting in order, but whenever a question caught my attention I've written to someone and received an answer. I have documents to support me. Now, how do you organize yours?”
“Partly in pigeonholes,” Mr. Casaubon replied, looking rather startled by the effort required.
“Ah, pigeonholes won't do. I've tried those, but everything gets muddled in them. I never know whether a paper is under A or Z.”
“I wish you'd let me organize your papers, uncle,” Dorothea said. “I'd give them all letters and then list the subjects under each one.”
Mr. Casaubon smiled in solemn approval and said to Mr. Brooke, “You see, you have an excellent secretary ready to hand.”
“No, no,” said Mr. Brooke with a shake of his head. “I can't have young ladies interfering with my documents. They're too flighty.”

Dorothea was hurt. Mr. Casaubon would suppose her uncle had some particular reason for saying this. In reality, the remark rested in his mind as lightly as a broken insect's wing among all its other scraps, and a passing current had blown it onto _her_.
Once the girls were alone together in the drawing room, Celia said—
“How dreadfully ugly Mr. Casaubon is!”
“Celia! He's one of the most distinguished-looking men I've ever seen. He looks remarkably like Locke's portrait. His eyes have those same deep sockets.”
“Did Locke have those two white moles with hairs growing out of them?”
“Oh, very likely! When a certain sort of person looked at him,” Dorothea replied, walking a little way off.
“Mr. Casaubon has such a yellow complexion.”
“So much the better. I suppose you prefer a man with skin like a _cochon de lait_.”
“Dodo!” Celia exclaimed, watching her in surprise. “I've never heard you compare anyone to that before.”
“Why would I have said it before I had a reason? It's a good comparison. The likeness is exact.”
Miss Brooke was plainly forgetting her manners, and Celia thought so too.
“I'm surprised at you losing your temper, Dorothea.”
“It's so painful, Celia, that you insist on seeing human beings as nothing more than dressed-up animals, and never recognize a great soul in a man's face.”
“Does Mr. Casaubon have a great soul?” There was a little innocent malice in Celia's question.
“Yes, I believe he does,” Dorothea answered in a firm, full voice. “Everything I observe in him agrees with his pamphlet on Biblical Cosmology.”
“He doesn't say very much,” Celia remarked.
“He has nobody here he can talk to.”

Celia thought privately, “Dorothea quite despises Sir James Chettam. I don't believe she'd accept him.” She felt that was a pity. She had never mistaken the object of the baronet's interest. Sometimes she had reflected that Dodo might not make a husband happy if he did not share her outlook. Buried deep in her heart was the feeling that her sister was too religious for a comfortable family life. Her principles and scruples were like spilled needles, making one afraid to walk, to sit, or even to eat.

When Miss Brooke sat at the tea table, Sir James came to sit beside her, having found nothing offensive in her earlier answers. Why would he? He thought she probably liked him, and behaviour must be very emphatic before people stop interpreting it through their own confident or suspicious expectations. She charmed him completely, though naturally he had formed a little theory about his attachment. He was made of excellent human dough and had the rare virtue of knowing that his abilities, even unleashed, would not set the smallest stream in the county on fire. So he liked the prospect of a wife he could ask, “What shall we do?” about one thing or another; someone who could supply her husband with reasons, and whose property would also qualify her to do so. As for Miss Brooke's alleged excess of religion, his idea of what it amounted to was very vague, and he expected marriage to extinguish it. In short, he felt he had fallen in love in the right quarter and was prepared to accept a great deal of female ascendancy, which a man, after all, could always suppress whenever he chose. Sir James could not imagine ever wishing to suppress this handsome girl's ascendancy; her cleverness delighted him. Why shouldn't it? A man's mind—whatever there is of it—always has the advantage of being male, just as the smallest birch belongs to a higher order than the loftiest palm. Even his ignorance is of a sounder kind. Sir James may not have invented this judgment, but a kindly Providence provides even the limpest personality with a little stiffening glue or starch in the shape of tradition.
“I hope you'll reconsider your decision about the horse, Miss Brooke,” her persistent admirer said. “I assure you, there's no healthier exercise than riding.”
“I know that,” Dorothea answered coldly. “I think it would benefit Celia—if she would take it up.”
“But you're such an accomplished rider yourself.”
“Forgive me, but I've had very little practice, and a horse could throw me easily.”
“Then you have all the more reason to practise. Every lady should be an accomplished rider so that she can ride with her husband.”

“You see how far apart our views are, Sir James. I've decided I ought not to become an accomplished rider, so I'd never fit your ideal of a lady.” Dorothea stared straight ahead and spoke with chilly abruptness, looking very much like a handsome boy. The contrast with her admirer's anxious good nature was amusing.
“I'd like to know what reasons you have for such a cruel decision. Surely you can't think riding is wrong.”
“It's perfectly possible for me to think it would be wrong for me.”
“But why?” Sir James protested in a gentle, tender voice.
Mr. Casaubon had approached the table with his teacup and stood listening.

“We should not probe motives too closely,” he interjected in his measured manner. “Miss Brooke knows they tend to weaken when expressed: their fragrance mingles with the coarser air. We must keep the sprouting seed out of the light.”

Dorothea flushed with pleasure and looked up at him gratefully. Here was a man who understood the higher inward life, with whom spiritual communion was possible; more than that, who could illuminate moral principle with the broadest knowledge. His learning almost proved the truth of whatever he believed!

Dorothea's conclusions may seem sweeping, but life could hardly have continued in any age without this generous allowance of inferences, which makes marriage possible amid civilization's difficulties. Has anyone ever squeezed the cobweb of premarital acquaintance down to the tiny pill it really amounts to?
“Certainly,” the good Sir James agreed. “We mustn't press Miss Brooke for reasons she'd prefer not to discuss. I'm sure they would do her credit.”

He felt no jealousy at the interest in Dorothea's upward glance towards Mr. Casaubon. It never entered his head that a girl he was considering marrying could care for a dried-up bookworm approaching fifty, except in a religious sort of way, as she might for a clergyman of some standing.

Still, since Miss Brooke had begun talking to Mr. Casaubon about the Vaudois clergy, Sir James went over to Celia and spoke to her about her sister. He mentioned a house in town and asked whether Miss Brooke disliked London. Away from Dorothea, Celia talked freely, and Sir James reflected that the younger Miss Brooke was certainly very agreeable as well as pretty, though not, as some claimed, cleverer or more sensible than her older sister. He felt he had chosen the one who was superior in every respect. Naturally a man likes to expect the best. A bachelor who pretended not to would be a very Mawworm of hypocrisy.
